title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: One of Anna's reasons for coming back to Russia had been to see her son. From the day she'd left Italy the thought of it had never stopped agitating her. The closer she got to Petersburg, the greater the joy and importance of the meeting grew in her imagination. She didn't even ask herself how to arrange it. It seemed natural and simple to her — she would see her son once she was in the same city as him. But on arriving in Petersburg she was suddenly made sharply aware of her present position in society, and grasped that arranging this meeting was no easy matter.

She had been in Petersburg for two days now. The thought of her son hadn't left her for a moment, but she hadn't yet seen him. Going straight to the house, where she might run into Alexey Alexandrovitch — that, she felt, she had no right to do. She might be turned away and insulted. Writing to him, and so opening up some kind of relationship with her husband — that was misery just to think about; she could only be at peace when she didn't think of her husband at all. Catching a glimpse of her son out walking — finding out where and when he went out — wasn't enough; she had looked forward to this meeting so much, she had so much to say to him, she so longed to hold him and kiss him. Seryozha's old nurse might be able to help and tell her what to do. But the nurse no longer lived at Alexey Alexandrovitch's house. In all this uncertainty, and in trying to track down the nurse, two days had slipped past.

Having heard about the close friendship between Alexey Alexandrovitch and Countess Lidia Ivanovna, Anna decided on the third day to write the countess a letter, which cost her great effort, and in which she said pointedly that permission to see her son must rest on her husband's generosity. She knew that if the letter were shown to her husband, he would keep up his pose of magnanimity and would not refuse her request.

The messenger who took the letter brought back the most cruel, unexpected answer: there was no answer. She had never felt so humiliated as the moment when, summoning the messenger, she heard from him the exact account of how he had waited, and how he had then been told there was no answer. Anna felt humiliated, insulted, but she saw that from her own point of view Countess Lidia Ivanovna was in the right. Her pain was sharper because she had to bear it alone. She couldn't and wouldn't share it with Vronsky. She knew that to him — though he was the original cause of her distress — the question of seeing her son would seem trivial. She knew that he would never be capable of understanding the depth of her suffering, that his cool tone at the slightest mention of it would make her start to hate him. And she dreaded that more than anything in the world, so she hid from him everything to do with her son. She spent the entire day at home, turning over ways of seeing him, and had decided to write to her husband. She was actually composing the letter when Lidia Ivanovna's reply was handed to her. The countess's silence had subdued and depressed her, but the letter — everything she read between its lines — so infuriated her, this malice was so revolting set against her passionate, lawful tenderness for her son, that she turned against everyone else and stopped blaming herself.

"This coldness — this performance of feeling!" she said to herself. "They have to insult me and torture the child, and I'm supposed to put up with it! Under no circumstances! She's worse than I am. At least I don't lie." And on the spot she decided that the next day, Seryozha's birthday, she would go straight to her husband's house, bribe or trick the servants — whatever it took — see her son, and overturn the hideous fiction they were wrapping the unhappy child in.

She went to a toy shop, bought toys, and thought through her plan. She would go early in the morning at eight o'clock, when Alexey Alexandrovitch was sure not to be up. She'd have money ready to give the hall-porter and the footman so they would let her in. Without lifting her veil, she would say she'd come from Seryozha's godfather to wish him a happy birthday and had been asked to leave the toys by his bedside. She had worked out everything except the words she would say to her son. As often as she'd dreamed of it, she still couldn't think of anything to say.
The next morning at eight, Anna got out of a hired sledge and rang at the front door of her former home.

"Go and see what they want. Some lady," said Kapitonitch — who, not yet dressed, in his overcoat and galoshes, had peeped out of the window and spotted a veiled lady standing right at the door. His assistant, a boy Anna didn't know, had hardly opened the door for her before she stepped inside and quickly pressed a three-rouble note from her muff into his hand.
"Seryozha — Sergey Alexeitch," she said, and was about to walk on. Studying the note, the porter's assistant stopped her at the second glass door.
"Who do you want to see?" he asked.
She didn't take in his words and gave no answer.
Noticing the strange lady's confusion, Kapitonitch came over to her, opened the second door for her, and asked what she would like.
"From Prince Skorodumov for Sergey Alexeitch," she said.
"He's not up yet," said the porter, looking at her closely.

Anna hadn't expected that the entirely unchanged front hall of the house where she had lived for nine years would affect her so much. Memories, sweet and painful, rose up one after another in her heart, and for a moment she forgot what she was there for.
"Would you mind waiting?" said Kapitonitch, taking off her fur cloak.
As he removed the cloak, Kapitonitch glanced at her face, recognized her, and made her a low, silent bow.
"Please come in, your excellency," he said.

She tried to say something, but no sound would come; with a guilty, pleading glance at the old man she went up the stairs with light, swift steps. Bent over, his galoshes catching on the steps, Kapitonitch ran after her, trying to keep up.
"The tutor's in there. He may not be dressed. I'll let him know."
Anna kept climbing the familiar staircase, not taking in what the old man was saying.

"This way, to the left, if you please. Excuse the state of it. His honor's in the old parlor now," the hall-porter said, out of breath. "Excuse me, wait just a moment, your excellency. I'll go and check," he said, and overtaking her, opened the high door and disappeared behind it. Anna stood waiting. "He's only just woken up," the hall-porter said as he came back out. And at the very moment the porter said this, Anna caught the sound of a child's yawn. From the sound of that yawn alone she recognized her son and seemed to see him alive in front of her.

"Let me in. Go away!" she said, and walked in through the high doorway. To the right of the door stood a bed, and the boy was sitting up in it. His little body bent forward, his nightshirt unbuttoned, he was stretching and still yawning. The instant his lips came together they curled into a blissful, sleepy smile, and with that smile he slowly and deliciously rolled back again.
"Seryozha!" she whispered, going noiselessly up to him.

While they had been apart, and all through the recent weeks when she'd been feeling a fresh surge of love for him, she had pictured him as he had been at four — the age she had loved him most. Now he wasn't even what he'd been when she left him; he was further still from the four-year-old, taller and thinner. How thin his face was, how short his hair was cut! What long hands! How he'd changed since she left him! But it was still him — his head, his lips, his soft neck, his broad little shoulders.
"Seryozha!" she said again, right by the child's ear.

He propped himself up on his elbow again, turned his tangled head from side to side as if searching for something, and opened his eyes. Slowly, questioningly, he looked for a few seconds at his mother standing motionless before him, and then all at once he broke into a blissful smile, and shutting his eyes, rolled — not back, but toward her, into her arms.

"Seryozha! My darling boy!" she said, breathing hard and wrapping her arms around his plump little body. "Mother!" he said, wriggling about in her arms so as to touch her hands with every part of him at once.

Still smiling sleepily with his eyes closed, he flung his fat little arms around her shoulders, rolled toward her with the delicious sleepy warmth and smell only children have, and started rubbing his face against her neck and shoulders.
"I know," he said, opening his eyes. "It's my birthday today. I knew you'd come. I'll get up in a minute."
And with that he fell asleep.

Anna looked at him hungrily; she saw how he had grown and changed in her absence. She both knew and didn't know those bare legs, so long now, sticking out from under the quilt — those short-cropped curls on his neck where she had kissed him so often. She touched all of this and could say nothing; tears were choking her.
"What are you crying about, mother?" he said, waking up fully. "Mother, what are you crying about?" he called in a tearful voice.

"I won't cry.… I'm crying for joy. It's been so long since I've seen you. I won't, I won't," she said, swallowing back the tears and turning her face away. "Come on, it's time for you to get dressed," she added after a moment, and, never letting go of his hands, sat down on the chair by his bed where his clothes had been laid out.
"How do you get dressed without me? How…?" She tried to start chatting simply and brightly, but she couldn't, and again she had to turn away.
"I don't take cold baths. Papa didn't order them. And have you not seen Vassily Lukitch yet? He'll be in soon. Look — you're sitting on my clothes!"
And Seryozha burst into a peal of laughter. She looked at him and smiled.
"Mother, darling, sweet one!" he cried, throwing himself on her again and hugging her. It was as if only now, seeing her smile, did he fully realize what had happened.
"I don't want that on you," he said, lifting off her hat. And as though seeing her freshly without it, he fell to kissing her all over again.
"But what did you think about me? You didn't think I was dead?"
"I never believed it."
"You didn't believe it, sweetheart?"
"I knew, I knew!" he repeated, his favorite phrase, and snatching the hand that was stroking his hair, he pressed the open palm to his mouth and kissed it.
